extracted.intended_audience: Citizens, voters, and policymakers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (historical audience: People of the State of New York)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and concrete provisions for constituting a federal judiciary: how judges are appointed and paid, their tenure and removability, the scope of federal jurisdiction, and institutional safeguards to secure judicial independence and impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of appointing judges
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of appointing the judges is the same with that of appointing the officers of the Union in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointment mechanism follows the general scheme previously discussed (President with Senate advice/consent as in the Convention's plan). The page notes this point has been fully discussed earlier and need not be repeated here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure 'during good behavior' (permanency in office)
rubrics_metrics.description: All judges appointed by the United States are to hold their offices DURING GOOD BEHAVIOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permanency is presented as indispensable to secure 'a steady, upright, and impartial administration of the laws.' It protects judges from encroachments by the legislature and executive, fosters independence, and is termed 'the citadel of the public justice and the public security.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence as essential (weakest branch needs protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary, from the nature of its functions, will always be the least dangerous to the political rights of the Constitution; it has neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment, and must depend on the executive for the efficacy of its judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the judiciary lacks force and purse, special institutional safeguards (permanency, non-diminishable compensation, impartial appointment) are required to prevent it from being overpowered, awed, or influenced by the other branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (judging distinct from legislature and executive)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no liberty if the power of judging be not separated from the legislative and executive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must be distinct to protect liberty; union with either other department would endanger rights. Independence of judges ensures enforcement of constitutional limitations such as prohibitions on bills of attainder and ex post facto laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review — courts may declare legislative acts void
rubrics_metrics.description: Every act of a delegated authority contrary to the tenor of the commission under which it is exercised is void; no legislative act contrary to the Constitution can be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power does not imply judicial superiority over the legislature but reflects the duty to prefer the Constitution (the people's will) to statutes (agents' will). Courts are the proper intermediaries to ascertain meaning of the Constitution and statutes and to choose the superior law when they conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges as interpreters of the Constitution (constitution as fundamental law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges, as a fundamental law; it therefore belongs to them to ascertain its meaning, as well as the meaning of any particular act proceeding from the legislative body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges should regulate their decisions by the Constitution rather than by ordinary statutes. The courts are characterized as an intermediate body between the people and the legislature to keep the latter within assigned limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed provision for judges' support (non-diminishable compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges shall at stated times receive for their services a compensation which shall not be diminished during their continuance in office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial dependence on the legislature undermines independence. Compensation may be adjusted upward by legislature as circumstances change, but cannot be reduced for a sitting judge. This differs from the President (whose compensation neither increased nor diminished during term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility via impeachment (limited means of removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Precautions for judges' responsibility are comprised in the article respecting impeachments: they are liable to be impeached for malconduct by the House and tried by the Senate; if convicted, may be dismissed and disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impeachment is portrayed as the only provision consistent with necessary judicial independence. Other modes of removal (for inability, etc.) are rejected as either impracticable or liable to abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special removal-for-inability mechanism (against age-limits and vague tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a provision for removing judges on account of inability has been a subject of complaint, but such provision would either not be practiced upon or would be more liable to abuse than to answer any good purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mensuration of mental faculties is not a known art; attempts to fix boundaries (e.g., mandatory retirement at 60) are condemned as arbitrary, unjust, and improper—they would injure deserving judges who retain faculties and livelihoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of federal judicature — proper objects (six descriptive categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary authority of the Union ought to extend to: (1) cases arising out of the laws of the United States; (2) cases concerning the execution of the articles of Union; (3) cases in which the United States are a party; (4) cases involving the peace of the Confederacy (intercourse with foreign nations or between States); (5) cases originating on the high seas/admiralty; (6) cases in which State tribunals cannot be supposed impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category is justified: (1) to give efficacy to constitutional provisions; (2) because judicial power should be coextensive with legislative power for uniform interpretation; (3) controversies involving the nation require national tribunals; (4) foreign relations and inter-State peace require federal cognizance; (5) maritime causes implicate laws of nations and foreigners; (6) where state bias exists (e.g., inter-state land grants) neutral national tribunals are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated constitutional jurisdiction (cases listed in plan of convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal jurisdiction as stated: 'all cases in law and equity arising under the Constitution, the laws of the United States, and treaties...; cases affecting ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls; admiralty and maritime jurisdiction; controversies to which the United States shall be a party; controversies between two or more States; between a State and citizens of another State; between citizens of different States; between citizens of the same State claiming lands under grants of different States; and between a State or the citizens thereof and foreign states, citizens, and subjects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list 'constitutes the entire mass of the judicial authority of the Union' and is to be reviewed and tested against the principles earlier discussed. The paper distinguishes 'arising under the Constitution' from 'arising under the laws of the United States' by example (e.g., prohibitions on states to emit paper money).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of interpretation — federal judiciary coextensive with legislative power
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of the judicial power of a government being coextensive with its legislative may be ranked among political axioms; the mere necessity of uniformity in the interpretation of the national laws decides the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple final courts (one per state) for the same national law would produce contradiction and confusion; a national tribunal ensures uniform legal interpretation across the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal tribunals for interstate and foreign disputes to preserve public peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of determining causes between States, between a State and citizens of another, and between citizens of different States, is essential to the peace of the Union; cases involving foreigners should be referred to national tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: History (e.g., Germanic body) shows the need for a central court to prevent private wars; foreign grievances may implicate sovereigns and treaties, so national courts are most appropriate. Distinctions between cases touching laws of nations versus municipal law may be impracticable, so broad federal jurisdiction is safer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction where state tribunals are biased or have local attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where State tribunals cannot be supposed to be impartial and unbiased (e.g., claims to land under grants of different States), federal courts are proper tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local attachments and prejudices in state courts (and law prejudging questions) make them unfit to decide controversies involving other States or their citizens; a national tribunal with no local attachments will be more impartial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of preference in conflicting laws (interpretive principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two statutes of equal authority conflict, the last in order of time shall be preferred; but between the interfering acts of a superior and subordinate authority, the prior act of the superior ought to be preferred to the subsequent act of the inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rule of construction adopted by courts: it is not positive law but derives from reason. Practically, the Constitution (superior) prevails over subsequent statutes (inferior). The courts' duty is to adhere to the Constitution and disregard contrary statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of precedent and specialized legal knowledge — need to attract qualified judges
rubrics_metrics.description: A voluminous code of laws requires strict rules and precedents; records of precedents will swell and demand long and laborious study to acquire competent knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A temporary duration in office would discourage capable lawyers from accepting the bench and would reduce the quality of justice. Permanency helps retain learned, upright judges necessary for interpreting complex and voluminous legal materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judicial dependence on legislative grants for subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: A power over a man's subsistence amounts to a power over his will; leaving the judiciary dependent for pecuniary resources on occasional grants of the legislature undermines separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Salaries should be protected (not diminished) so that judges cannot be coerced or influenced by legislative control over funding; permanent salaries in words alone have proven insufficient without explicit non-diminution protections.
